title: Poems and Letters of Harriet Wilson
description: Scattered poems, letters and religious verses composed from the 1850s onward and recovered by modern scholarship: the small surviving body of Wilson's occasional writing. It is a verse work of 1850 by Harriet E. Wilson; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under dialect poem and vernacular performance; review essay and quarterly argument.

meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in dialect and vernacular: the spelling carries the pronunciation, the stanza is song-like and often rhymed in ballad measure, and the poem is written to be spoken or performed aloud. The text is cast as letters, the argument carried by correspondence. The author's characteristic manner is first-person and third-person autobiographical narrative.

The record dates the work as composed between 1850 and 1900 and first published in 1850 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under dialect poem and vernacular performance; review essay and quarterly argument.

bibliographical_notes: First published in 1850, as poems, letters and occasional prose, by Harriet E. Wilson. Composed between 1850 and 1900. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

principal_characters: Currer; Clotel; Thomas Jefferson; Horatio Green; Althesa; Henry; Mary; George Green; Nat Turner
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. title: A Voice from the South

plot_or_argument: Cooper argues that the black woman is the pivot of racial progress, that the black church and the black man have failed to support her education, that the women's movement must include black women, and that the South's future depends on the cultivation of its women; the essays range over literature, religion, politics and education.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.

title: Southern Horrors: Lynch Law in All Its Phases

title: The Reason Why the Colored American Is Not in the World's Columbian Exposition

title: 'The Outcasts of Poker Flat'
